subject: Climate & Environment
title: Wildfires and Climate Change
description: A short lesson to help you apply Wildfires and Climate Change.

hook.text: In 2020, Australia's wildfires burned 46 million acres — an area the size of Syria.

buildup.text: Hotter, drier conditions extend fire seasons and make forests more flammable each year.

discovery.text: Fires release the carbon that forests spent decades storing, pushing warming even further.

twist.text: Burned forests regrow slowly. Some are too damaged to return at all and become grassland.

climax.text: Climate change creates more fires, and more fires accelerate climate change — a vicious loop.

punchline.text: Fire is natural. The scale we are seeing is not.

quiz.question: How does climate change affect wildfires?
options: Hotter, drier conditions make forests more flammable

details.summary: Climate change is making forests more flammable by raising temperatures, extending droughts, and drying fuels earlier. The resulting increase in wildfire frequency and intensity turns forests from carbon sinks into carbon sources and creates dangerous feedback loops.
details.whyItMatters: Fire and climate change reinforce each other. More warming means more fire, which releases more carbon, which drives more warming. Breaking this cycle requires both fire management and emission cuts.
takeaways: Global area burned by wildfires has been increasing since 2000
Fire emissions in some years rival entire countries' fossil fuel output
Climate-driven fires are pushing fire into previously non-fire-prone forests

faq.question: Are wildfires always destructive?
faq.answer: Many ecosystems evolved with periodic fire that clears undergrowth and recycles nutrients. The problem is when fires burn too frequently or intensely due to climate change and fuel buildup, exceeding ecosystems' capacity to recover.

faq.question: How much CO2 do wildfires release?
faq.answer: Global wildfires release roughly 5 to 8 billion tons of CO2 per year. Much is reabsorbed by regrowth, but climate-intensified fires that burn deeper into peat and soil release carbon that takes centuries to replace.
